posts.content_md:
I was working with POV-Ray, and while it should be intuitive I never really thought about it. If you are trying to get actual meter Power Density readings at you plate and you point your meter head to the light source, measure the Power and then calculate the detector head are to conver to cm^2 you will be off. 

That is if your dector head area is 1cm x 1cm or 1cm^2 and your beam in coming in at a 56 degree angle but you measure power with detector head perpendicular the calculations will be incorrect. Because the plate is receiving light at an angle this angle needs to be factored in in the one direction of the area caculation of the meter head area. The differece is pretty sizable.

Here is an illustration that I think may help explain this.

![Image](http://www.holograms3d.com/Illustrations/MeterHeadArea.jpg)

posts.author: wler
posts.post_subject: Meter Head Correction for Measuring Actual Power Density
posts.content_md:
If you tilt your plate by 56 degrees so that the ref beam comes from the side, the actual power density in uW/cm^2 on the plate is approx 1/2 of what you measure with a detector when facing the ref beam. So if you aim at a certain value of exposure, you need to take this factor into account (the exposure curves on my site include it).

The object light comes in straight, so that will be measured correctly. On the other hand, the variations across the plate will be large anyway.

So all-in-all, the procedure I follow is:

1) measure ref beam intensity R with detector perpendicular to the beam

2) measure object beam intensity O in the brightest region, with detector facing the object

3) tune to a good beam ratio, O=1/4 R, say

then total exposure is O+1/2 R = 3/4 R

posts.topic_title: Meter Head Correction for Measuring Actual Power Density
posts.author: BobH
posts.post_subject: Meter Head Correction for Measuring Actual Power Density
posts.content_md:
> I think we went around this a while ago with Bob H and Kaveh and I when discussing beam balance ratios. If the holoplate or power meter is tilted, it receives less energy as you have stated. Power readings should have the detector parallel to the plate, the same way the light is hitting the light-sensitive material.

I still disagree. 

When building a set-up, we split the the light and recombine it at the recording plane. Before a piece of film is placed in the plateholder, the interference fringes exist in space where the two beams overlap. If we want to maximize the fringe visibility there, we want to set the beam ratio to one. This is done by measuring the power in each beam and making them equal.

The visibility of the fringes has nothing to do with the orientation of a recording plane intersecting them. That's why I believe that measuring the beams (for the purpose of setting the beam ratio) is best done with the detector perpendicular to the beam. We want (for maximum fringe visibility) the amplitudes of the two beams to be equal.

Now, if we place a piece of film in the plateholder, each beam hits the plate at some angle. If we want to expose the plate properly, we need to know the total *energy density* hitting the plate. I suppose that making *this* measurement is best done with the detector parallel to the recording plane. Real detectors (that I'm aware of), however, are mounted within their housings, which usually vignettes the beam being measured. This is especially true when making edge-illuminated holograms. 

Since flush mounted detectors are not available, and measuring for proper exposure is usually simply a starting point for an "exposure bracket", I recommend always measuring with the detector pointed directly into the beam being measured. This gives accurate control of fringe visibility via beam ratio, which is especially important in an image-planed transfer set-up where the localized beam ratios vary widely.

posts.topic_title: Meter Head Correction for Measuring Actual Power Density
posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.post_subject: Meter Head Correction for Measuring Actual Power Density
posts.content_md:
The correction factor for the difference between having the light hit the detector along the normal versus the actual angle of incidence is the cosine of the angle of incidence. That's the trig function which starts with cos 0 degrees = 1, and then gets smaller until you hit 90 degrees. Multiply the power reading at the normal by the cosine of the angle of the plate and you will get a better reading.

Sometimes you hear that the real reading is cos^2 but I haven't seen that documented anywhere.

Yeah, I thought of the recess problem after I had posted previously. It's hard to believe that so many of these manufacturers of expensive power meters don't think of what are the typical applications and deeply recess the cells so that we can't take true readings at typical angles of incidence. There was a Coherent 212 I worked with a Newport 820, and they both had this problem.

I feel that there is no doubt that to get the proper exposure reading the power meter detector should be parallel to the plate because of the loss of power due to reflection and angle of incidence. Previously Bob and Kaveh and I had gone around about the beam balance ratio and measurements to determining it. The I guess we all got busy and nothing was resolved. 

I still think that even the BBR needs to be measured with the detector parallel to the plate for practical purposes because of mainly the reflection losses as the beams go into the emulsion. In air, that's a different story.

But in the end, whatever works best, and you can do consistently is the solution!

Yes! 

Well, maybe. I just reviewed Mitch Henrion's M.S. thesis for MIT titled "Diffraction and Exposure Characteristics of the Edgelit Hologram". In it she discusses this very topic, related to edgelit holograms because their extreme geometry forces the issue.

Her conclusion is that the beams should be measured with the detector pointing directly toward the source. Detectors are all designed to be used that way, for good reason. For "effective exposure energy" calculation, however, she recommends multiplying the measured reference beam by the cosine of the angle of incidence. Apparently a good compromise between Ed's and my positions.

Is a beam ratio (so not the absolute intensity of the reference beam) not always measured with the meter towards the source of the light? That would seem logical to me because the absolute intensity of the brightest fringes doesn't change with the orientation of the plate.

In that case it would seem logical to me to measure the ratio's towards the light sources and use the amount of light reflected of the object for determining the exposure time. However, that brings a new question to my mind: What do we measure to determine the exposure time for our plates? Do we measure the intensity of the reference beam, the object beam, or the brightest fringes? I would think that the only thing that counts is the brightest fringes, and they can be brighter than the reference beam, am I right?

But also a new question comes to mind: Would the angle between the reference beam and the object beam not be more important to the brightness of the fringes than the angle of the plate? What I mean to say here is that if the angle was 0 degrees, there would only be one theoretical very long fringe, smeared out in the direction of the beams. But if they collided at 180 degrees, as with a Denisyuk with a 0 degrees to normal reference beam, the fringes would be very thin. But will they also be brighter?

The fringes are, I guess impossible to measure. But with a beam ratio of, for example, 1:1 the fringes can be twice as bright as the reference beam. So it must be easy to calculate them for other ratio's. How wide are the fringes? The emulsion is not infinitly thin, so the fringes are not smeared out on the plate like sun light hitting the Earth at an angle, but they penetrate the emulsion and also do their work there. Are they wider than the thickness of the emulsion? If not, I would think that the orientation of the plate will not matter because the fringes will fit entirely inside the emulsion. So in that case we should be able to determine the exposure time by aiming the meter towards the reference beam again, and then shortening the exposure time by a factor that is determined by the beam ratio (1:1 beam ratio -> half the exposure time, 1:0 beam ratio -> full exposure time). Can it not be that simple? I am reasoning here with my very limited knowledge. 

Well, it's just me doing thought experiments here. I am still waiting for my copy of Bjelkhagen from Amazon (2 months late now).

posts.content_md:
Edgelit holograms are those whose reconstruction beam is within the TIR conditions of the hologram material or base. That can be from 45 degrees to 89 degrees. 

Your points about using the "brightness of the fringes" for exposure calculation is probably theoretically correct thinking, but impractical in the real world. I think so many things affect optimum exposure for a pictorial hologram that this level of detail is lost in the noise. 

Consistancy of technique is the most important thing for individual workers, I think. Also, a healthy skepticism regarding reports of optimum beam ratios or exposure energy (or times) is a good thing. Nothing beats personal experimentation. 

"Good judgement comes from experience. Experience comes from bad judgement."

posts.content_md:
I just thought of a new thought experiment in the shape of a fairy tale on my way back from the fast food place. 

I imagine I were really really small. I was so small, about the size of a AgBr grain. In fact, I was one. I was so small, that I could not even see myself in the mirror. That being the fact, I could not even know if I was wearing a baseball cap or not! 

But luckily there was a solution to that: 

I was suspended in a theoretically ideally transparent gelatin base. All alone... Someone decided to shine a laser beam through the emulsion. If I would be entirely inside the laser beam, I would loose a few electrons and the great developer man would give me a suntan. It did not really matter at all at what angle the laser beam would hit my body because the gelatin was completely transparent. The only effect the leaser beam angle would have was the rate at wich a NON-transparent emulsion would heat up, or block the light from hitting my body. But with the perfectly transparent emulsion, the same amount of laser light would hit my body, no matter what angle...

Thinking about this story, it seems to me that it makes absolutely no difference at all at what angle any beam hits the plate, as long as there were only one AgBr grain and the gelatin were ferfectly transparent. However the gelatin is not transparent. If the light enters the gelatin at an angle, it will be attenuated slightly because of the longer travel distance through the gelatin. If there are more AgBr grains, again an angle would be bad because the other grains will scatter or capture the light before it hits my body. So, it seems to me that there are several factors determining the correlation between exposure time and illumination angle:

- The transparency of the gelatin.

- The size of the AgBr grains.

- The amount (density) of AgBr grains in the emulsion.

- The thickness of the emulsion.

What I mean to say is like this: In the early morning I cannot get much of a suntan because of the longer travel distance of the sun light through the atmosphere. But if I was standing on the moon, or if I were on the top of a mountain, the time of day (angle of the sun) would make no difference because there is no atmosphere to absorb/scatter the sun light. The only thing that would matter now was the orientation of my body in relation to the sun. But as the AgBr grains are (I guess) randomly oriented in the gelatin, that is no factor.

posts.content_md:
I have just been thinking some more about that cosine factor with relation to reference beam angle. Perhaps she meant the following:

-Suppose the light-attenuation factor (due to absorbtion and scattering) of the emulsion is: **A %/meter traveled**

-Suppose the thickness of the emulsion is: **t meter**

-Suppose the angle of the reference beam is: **q**

-Suppose the height of the plate is: **h** meter

-Suppose the intensity of the light is: **I** Watt/cm*cm

The light intensity of the light that is about to exit the other side of the emulsion would then be: i= max{h*A, A*t*cos(q)}*I; The h*A term is the limiting factor here when the light enters the emulsion through it's edge.

I have not taken into account the amount of light reflected off the plate from the reference beam here, which also changes with the reference angle.

So, I would think that the light intensity should always be measured towards the light source. The light attenuation of the plate+gelatin with relation to the reference angle can be measured for this type of plate for several angles and plotted into a graph.

Then one could use a simple five step procedure right?

1: Determine beam ratio's.

2: Determine intensity of the reference beam with the meter pointed towards it.

3: Calculate intensity of the strongest fringes, according to beam ratio and reference beam intensity.

4: Determine attenuation from the plotted graph.

5: Decide about the exposure time accordingly.

This way the part of the emulsion where the reference beam exits will never be over exposed, but will allow for maximum exposure for that part of the emulsion that gets the least amount of light.

Again, I should say that I am severely limited by lack of knowledge. Just thought experimenting here.

posts.content_md:
It sounds like what you would like to know is how to find the change in area between a circle and when it is tranformed into an ellipse by tilting it so that its major axis is increased.

When the circular region in 3 space is rotated about one of its diameters, turning it into the new *minor axis*, the orthogonal radius becomes the *major axis*, and will be increased by the inverse of either the sine or cosine of the angle, depending on how you measure it.

If the circle is just sitting there minding its own business basking in the light waves arriving along its normal, then we say it's moved 0 degrees, so we use cosine, (since cos 0 degrees = 1, otherwise we run into a problem with dividing by sin 0 = 0) because we will be dividing the other diameter's measurement by the cosine of the angle that we have rotated it.

Tilting 30 degrees from the normal, the major axis grows by 1/cos 30 degrees or 1/.8660 = 1.155. Then this could be plugged into the area of an ellipse equation. Tilting more to 45 degrees gives a lengthening of the diameter by 1/.7071 or 1.414 times.

Notice the areas of the new ellipses compared to the original circle are off by a factor of, you guessed, the cosine of the angle of displacement from the normal! This is why the light meter's reading is attenuated, the area of radiant flux at right angles to the beam is now spread out over a larger area of the transformed ellipse! So there are less photons per unit area! Now does everyone see the wisdom of the detector parallel to the recording material?

What works out really really well for the new meter I have is that 

The opening is .5cm^2 thus the energy it reads needs to be doubled for cm^2 and holding the meter perpendicular to the beam while measureing the light in a SBR with the plate at 56 degrees means I have to halve the energy hitting the plate at that angle. Soooo....

What is read on the meter, at perpendicular to a Brewsters set up, is my actual power per cm^2. That is, if I read 25mW on the meter, then the plate is recieving 25mW/cm^2. This makes actual power measurement easy. Times that number by time and I have Joules.
